title: Rich Rebuilds paid $10,000 for a Rivian delivery van that powers up but won't drive
dek: A lemon-law buyback marked not for sale, the van is stuck on a parking-brake fault that only Rivian's own software can clear.

This van has no title paperwork, a not-for-sale flag and a fault it can't drive with. verdict: Not yet, and maybe never. On paper $10,000 for a van that cost about $80,000 new looks like a steal, and nearly every system works [1][5]. But a van that can't shift out of park, has no title and was flagged not for sale is worth little more than its parts until Rivian's software says otherwise. The build shows the new limit of salvage rebuilding: on a software-defined vehicle the hardest part to replace is access. If the factory tools clear the fault and a title follows, it pays handsomely; if not, it's an expensive lesson on camera.
body:
## The buy

Rich Benoit, who runs Rich Rebuilds, paid $10,000 for one of Rivian's electric delivery vans, the type Amazon runs in its fleet [1][2]. It isn't wearing Amazon livery, and the steering-wheel badge reads Rivian rather than Amazon, so it may never have delivered a parcel [1][3]. He bought it from a dealer, which had acquired it after the van went back to the maker under a lemon law: it had been broken from the start [1]. Rich said it came with no title and carried a "not for sale" marking [2]. He may be the first private, non-commercial owner of one [1][3].

For scale, Rivian's van started at about $80,000 to fleets; one sold new for $83,800 with destination [5]. His $10,000 is roughly an eighth of that.

## The damage

There is no crash damage. The van wakes up, the high-voltage system comes on, and the screens, lights and power doors work [1][2]. What it won't do is drive: its computers log a fault in the parking-brake system and refuse to put it in gear [1][3]. The seller had assumed it needed a new battery pack; Rich found the battery fine, and The Autopian says he was right [1].

The electric parking brake itself was inspected and appeared fine [1]. That leaves wiring, a module or software, and without Rivian's diagnostic tools the shop couldn't tell which [2]. The Autopian's Jason Torchinsky wrote that about 99% of the van seems to work but he wasn't confident it would drive again [7].

## The work and the parts

The September episode was mostly diagnosis [9]. Torque News reports no completed repairs and little useful service information for the van [2]. Gumtree's write-up frames the van as a right-to-repair warning: the remaining route was to ask Rivian for help, which it might refuse because of the not-for-sale flag [3].

The November episode moved it on. Its description says that after weeks of troubleshooting Rich finally got access to Rivian's factory software and started digging into the real problem, and that "things went south FAST" [4][10]. A Yahoo Autos headline says he borrowed parts from his own working Rivian to fix the van and ended up with two disabled vehicles [8]; we couldn't read that story, so we don't know which parts moved or whether the second vehicle was put right.

No part has been bought for the van that we know of. The parts list here is the diagnosis so far: a parking brake that tests fine, a battery that didn't need replacing, the factory software, and whatever was borrowed from his own Rivian.

## The money

In: $10,000, plus whatever software access and borrowed parts end up costing; none of that has been stated.

Out: running, titled used vans aren't cheap. A Ford dealer in Delaware lists four 2024 Rivian Delivery 500 step vans at $43,299 each, with 4,511 to 23,986 miles [6]. A nearly new 2025 Delivery 500 with 261 miles was bid to $49,000 on Bring a Trailer in September 2025 and didn't sell [5]. Those are working vans with titles. This one has neither working status nor paperwork, and a lemon-law history that has to be disclosed in most states once it is titled. We put it at about $8,000 as it sits and up to $35,000 if it drives and can be registered.

## What's next

The question is whether Rivian's factory software clears the fault or only explains it. If the van can be made to drive, the next hurdle is the paperwork: getting a title for a vehicle the maker marked not for sale. The Autopian suggests hackers could in theory reverse-engineer the software, but called that effort enormous [7]. We'll add the costs and the outcome as Rich states them.
